meta.title: Who really said "The natural healing force within each of us is the greatest force in getting well"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: No Hippocratic treatise contains this sentence. It is a modern wellness paraphrase of a real Hippocratic idea — nature as the body’s own physician.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'The natural healing force within each of us is the greatest force in getting well'?
meta.ogDescription: Hippocrates never wrote it. Classicist Helen King lists it among the internet’s Hippocrates sayings; the nearest genuine text is Epidemics VI.5.1.

answer.label: Not Hippocrates’ words — a modern paraphrase
answer.authorDates: c. 460 – c. 370 BC · Greek physician, the “Father of Medicine”
answer.sourceLine: No treatise in the Hippocratic Corpus contains this sentence, and it translates no known line of Greek. The classicist Helen King files it, in Hippocrates Now (Bloomsbury Academic, 2020) ↗, with “Let food be your medicine” and “Walking is the best medicine” among the sayings Hippocrates is supposed online to have uttered. The underlying idea is genuinely Hippocratic — Epidemics VI.5.1 opens by making the body’s own nature the physician in disease — but this English sentence is a modern wellness formulation laid over that idea, not a quotation of it.

source.excerpt: The natural healing force within each of us is the greatest force in getting well.
trail: Helen King, Hippocrates Now: The ‘Father of Medicine’ in the Internet Age (Bloomsbury Academic, 2020) ↗ opens with a 2017 fitness-industry article that runs this sentence next to “Let food be your medicine” and “Walking is the best medicine.” King’s whole subject is this class of sayings — things Hippocrates is credited with online rather than in any manuscript.

Wikiquote’s Hippocrates page ↗ cites its entries to named treatises and keeps a Disputed section for the well-known fakes (“Let food be thy medicine,” “Walking is man’s best medicine”). This line is not on the page at all — neither sourced nor disputed.

The Latin usually invoked alongside it, vis medicatrix naturae, is not attested in the Hippocratic corpus ↗; it is given there as the Latin form of the Greek Νóσων φύσεις ἰητροί, “Nature is the physician of diseases.”

Where the line does circulate, it circulates bare. Goodreads ↗ attaches no work, date or page and states that its quotes are added by members and not verified; AZQuotes ↗ prints the “each one of us” variant with no citation either.
source.excerptNote: Reproduced as it circulates. There is no fuller original context to show, because no ancient text reads like this; the common variant swaps “each of us” for “each one of us,” which is itself the mark of a saying passed hand to hand rather than copied off a page.

source.rightsNote: The wording has no identified author, work or first-publication date, so no copyright status can honestly be asserted for it. The ancient Greek of the Hippocratic Corpus is long out of copyright, but this English sentence is not a translation of any of it; the modern scholarship that documents its circulation — Helen King, Hippocrates Now (2020) — is in copyright and published under a Creative Commons Attribution-NonCommercial-NoDerivatives licence.

author.name: Hippocrates
author.heading: Who Hippocrates was
author.metaLine: c. 460 – c. 370 BC · Greek physician of Kos, the 'Father of Medicine'
author.bio: Hippocrates of Kos was a physician of the classical Greek period, remembered as the “Father of Medicine” for pushing the explanation of disease away from the supernatural and towards observation. The sixty-odd treatises gathered under his name were written by many hands, and Wikipedia’s survey of the scholarship notes that the authorship question has not been conclusively answered. That open-ended corpus is a large part of why almost any medical-sounding aphorism can be hung on him: there is no single book anyone can open to prove it is not there.

"The natural healing force within each of us is the greatest force in getting well" appears in no Hippocratic treatise and translates no known Greek line — it is a modern paraphrase of the Hippocratic idea of the body's own nature as the physician in disease (Epidemics VI.5.1). — Quotle.info

misattribution.heading: How it went wrong
misattribution.intro: Hippocrates is one of the most quoted figures in medicine and one of the least verifiable. Three separate things get folded together here.

items.why: It appears in no work of the Hippocratic Corpus and translates no surviving Greek line. Helen King’s study of the online Hippocrates ↗ opens with it as an example of what he is supposed to have said, quoted from a 2017 fitness-industry article alongside “Let food be your medicine.”

Vis medicatrix naturae is the phrase usually invoked when this idea is called Hippocratic, and it is not attested in his corpus ↗ either. King records that some scholars have traced the Latin form to the eighteenth-century physician William Cullen ↗.

“Let food be thy medicine and medicine be thy food” is the best-studied of these sayings: Wikiquote’s Disputed section ↗ records that it does not appear in the Hippocratic corpus, citing Diana Cardenas’s 2013 study in e-SPEN. “Walking is man’s best medicine” is listed there too.

misattribution.truthLine: The thought has a real ancestor. King ties the healing-power-of-nature idea to the opening of Epidemics VI.5.1 ↗, where the body’s own nature is cast as the physician in disease. What people share is a paraphrase of that idea, not a translation of it.

context.heading: Why this one sticks
lead: Hippocrates died around 370 BC and left, at most, a handful of the sixty-odd treatises that carry his name; the authorship question has never been conclusively settled ↗. That vagueness is exactly what makes him a magnet. A saying with no author can be handed to a name with no fixed corpus, and nobody can produce the page it is not on.

The line also does a specific job. Helen King’s study traces how the modern alternative-health movement adopted Hippocrates as its forefather through the popular literature of the twentieth century, reading him as the physician who trusted the body to heal itself. A sentence saying the healing force is within each of us is precisely the sentiment that movement needed, and an ancient Greek byline is what makes it sound settled rather than promotional.
context.detailsSummary: What the Hippocratic texts actually say about the body healing itself
detailsBody: The usual Latin shorthand for the idea is vis medicatrix naturae, “the healing power of nature”. Wikipedia records that the phrase is not attested in the Hippocratic corpus ↗ and presents it as the Latin form of the Greek Νóσων φύσεις ἰητροί, “Nature is the physician of diseases.”

King argues the tag has more Hippocratic warrant than it is usually given: those Greek words open the fifth section of Epidemics 6, where the body’s own physis is cast as the physician in disease and finds its way without instruction. She also notes that some scholars have traced the Latin phrasing itself to the eighteenth-century physician William Cullen ↗, not to antiquity.
context.pull: The idea is Hippocratic. The sentence is not.

sourcesVerified.claim: Helen King's Hippocrates Now (Bloomsbury Academic, London, first published 2020, CC BY-NC-ND) contains, in its Introduction, the sentence 'The natural healing force within each of us is the greatest force in getting well' listed among things Hippocrates is supposed to have said, alongside 'Let food be your medicine' and 'Walking is the best medicine', quoted from a 2017 Australian Fitness Network article; the book also states that vis medicatrix naturae is a tag sometimes traced back to Hippocrates, that some scholars have attributed the Latin form to the eighteenth-century William Cullen, and that the Greek Νόσων φύσεις ἰητροί translates the opening words of the fifth section of Epidemics 6 (Epidemics 6.5.1).

Wikiquote's Hippocrates page carries no quotation containing 'natural healing force' or 'greatest force in getting well' in any section; its Disputed section lists 'Let food be thy medicine and medicine be thy food' (citing Diana Cardenas, e-SPEN, 2013, as showing it does not appear in the Hippocratic corpus), 'Walking is man's best medicine', and 'It is quite as important to know what kind of a patient the disease has got'.

Wikipedia states that vis medicatrix naturae is the Latin rendering of the Greek Νόσων φύσεις ἰητροί ('Nature is the physician of diseases'), a phrase attributed to Hippocrates, and that the phrase is not actually attested in his corpus although it sums up a guiding principle of Hippocratic medicine.

Goodreads hosts the quote 'The natural healing force within each of us is the greatest force in getting well.' credited to Hippocrates with no book, work, page or other source citation, and states that quotes are added by the Goodreads community and are not verified by Goodreads.
AZQuotes hosts the variant 'The natural healing force within each one of us is the greatest force in getting well.' credited to Hippocrates with no book, publication, date or source citation.

Wikipedia gives Hippocrates' dates as c. 460 – c. 370 BC, describes him as a Greek physician regarded as the 'Father of Medicine', and states that the question of Hippocratic authorship of the corpus has not been conclusively answered, the collection likely comprising works by students and followers.
